title: Location and scale
overview: Location and scale shape cost, responsiveness, risk and long-run competitiveness. You must analyse local/national/international location decisions, offshoring and reshoring, globalisation, and internal/external economies and diseconomies of scale.
syllabusPoints: Analyse factors determining location and relocation at local, national and international levels.
Explain reasons for and impacts of offshoring and reshoring.
Analyse how globalisation changes location choices.
Explain internal/external economies of scale and diseconomies of scale and their effect on unit costs.

definitions.definition: Moving business activities or production to another country.
Returning previously offshored activity to the home country.
Reductions in average/unit cost as scale increases.
Increases in average/unit cost caused by excessive size/complexity.
Cost advantages gained because the industry/region grows, not because one firm alone becomes larger.

sections.title: Location factors
content: Important factors include labour skill/cost, land/rent, suppliers, transport, infrastructure, energy, customers, government incentives/tax, law/political stability and sustainability. Weighting depends on the business model—a data centre, luxury retailer and heavy manufacturer should not prioritise the same factors.

sections.title: Offshoring
content: Can lower labour/input cost, access specialist suppliers and place production nearer growing markets. Risks include longer supply chains, quality/control problems, exchange/political risk, cultural/communication issues and reputational concerns.

sections.title: Reshoring
content: May improve responsiveness, quality control, supply-chain resilience and home-market reputation. It can also increase direct labour/property cost. Automation can make reshoring more viable by reducing labour-cost differences.

sections.title: Globalisation and location
content: Trade liberalisation, digital coordination and global logistics allow firms to split design, production and service across countries. This increases choice but also creates dependence on international networks exposed to tariffs, pandemics, geopolitical tension and currency movement.

sections.title: Internal economies of scale
content: Purchasing (bulk discounts), technical (specialised machinery), managerial (specialist managers), financial (access/cost of finance), marketing (spread fixed promotion cost) and risk-bearing/diversification can reduce unit cost as the firm grows.

sections.title: External economies and diseconomies
content: Industry clusters can provide specialist labour, suppliers, infrastructure and knowledge. But very large businesses may suffer communication, coordination, motivation and bureaucracy problems, causing unit costs to rise. Growth is beneficial only while economies outweigh diseconomies.

analysisChains.title: Offshoring production
steps: The firm moves activity to a lower-cost country
Labour or operating costs may fall
Unit cost and price competitiveness improve
Supply-chain, quality and reputation risks increase
analysisChains.evaluation: The decision depends on total landed cost, reliability, skills, exchange rates and the strategic value of keeping production close to customers.

examTips: Location evaluation should weight the MOST important factors, not just list them.
Keep internal economies (firm growth) separate from external economies (industry/area growth).
Lowest wage cost does not necessarily mean lowest total operating cost.
commonMistakes: Treating outsourcing and offshoring as identical.
Calling any rise in total cost a diseconomy—diseconomies concern average/unit cost.
Assuming all large firms gain unlimited economies.
